assistant.primaryUsageNote: A slightly warmer and more polished alternative to "thanks" that still works in most casual contexts. For formal settings prefer "I appreciate it" or "much obliged".

alternativeTranslations.note: Sincere and warm; natural between friends or colleagues when you want to add weight.
Slightly more grown-up / professional feel; common in workplace chat and email.
Short and friendly: common in UK/Aus English, occasionally in US casual writing.

senses.definition: A short, informal expression of gratitude.
examples: Thanks, that's exactly what I needed.

senses.definition: An expression or feeling of gratitude.
examples: She sent her thanks in a handwritten card.

assistant.etymology: From Middle English thankes, from Old English þancas, plural of þanc "thought, gratitude."
assistant.notes: English has a wide casual-thanks vocabulary. "Ta" and "cheers" are British/Australian; "appreciate it" lands slightly more formal; "thanks so much" is universal.
